domains.name: Electrician Apprenticeship: etA Entrance
domains.summary: Everything a new apprentice needs before the first day on site: credentials, study skills, workplace conduct, finances, codes literacy, and the algebra behind the aptitude test.

scenarios.title: Reading the Code Like a Manual
scenarios.situation: You are handed your first excerpt from the National Electrical Code and told to find the rule that governs working-space clearances in front of an electrical panel. The Code is organized by numbered articles and chapters, and the index points you to Article 110.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most reliable first move when you need to locate a rule in the NEC?
choices: Use the Code's structure — start with the article the index or table of contents points to, then read the surrounding definitions and exceptions.
Memorize the article number now and skip reading; you can guess on the test.
Search the whole book front-to-back until a familiar word appears.
Ask a coworker for their interpretation and write that down as the rule.
scenarios.why: The NEC is a legal reference document, not a narrative textbook: its articles are the map. Article 110 covers requirements for electrical installations generally, and reading the full article — including its exceptions — prevents the classic apprentice error of applying a rule out of context. Speed comes later; accurate navigation is the skill being tested here.
scenarios.hint: Think of the NEC as a filing system, not a story. What tool does a filing system give you first?

scenarios.title: The Interim Credential Question
scenarios.situation: Your apprenticeship coordinator tells you that journeyman hours will take years to accumulate, but the training center offers interim credentials — short certifications like OSHA 10 and First Aid/CPR — that you can earn while your on-the-job hours grow.
scenarios.prompt: Why do interim credentials matter for an apprentice who has not yet qualified for a license?
choices: They document job-ready skills (safety, first response) that employers and programs can verify now, while license-required hours accumulate over time.
They replace the journeyman license, so you can skip the remaining hours.
They are only useful as wall decorations; employers ignore them.
They let you perform work reserved for licensed electricians unsupervised.
scenarios.why: Interim credentials are stackable proof of progress: OSHA 10 shows safety literacy, First Aid/CPR shows site readiness. They never substitute for licensure or required hours, but they keep a learner employable and auditable during the long middle of an apprenticeship — exactly the gap they are designed to bridge.
scenarios.hint: What does an employer need to believe about a first-year apprentice before trusting them on site?

scenarios.title: SQ3R on a Motor Nameplate Manual
scenarios.situation: Your instructor assigns a dense twelve-page motor-controller manual and says you will be tested on it tomorrow. You remember SQ3R: Survey, Question, Read, Recite, Review.
scenarios.prompt: Which sequence correctly applies SQ3R to this technical reading task?
choices: Survey the manual's headings and diagrams; turn each heading into a question; read to answer those questions; recite the answers from memory; review the manual again at the end.
Read every page twice, then re-read the hardest page a third time.
Skip to the test-relevant pages and ignore the rest to save time.
Highlight everything, then skim the highlights once before the test.
scenarios.why: SQ3R works because each step has a job: Survey builds the map, Question creates a retrieval target, Read fills it, Recite forces recall (the actual learning event), and Review locks it in. Passive highlighting skips the retrieval step entirely, which is why students who highlight heavily often feel prepared and still blank on the test.
scenarios.hint: Which step is the one where you close the manual and talk to yourself?

scenarios.title: When the Joke Stops Being a Joke
scenarios.situation: A senior journeyman keeps making comments about a coworker's appearance that make the whole crew uncomfortable. The coworker laughs along but later tells you they dread coming to work. You have a harassment-prevention orientation fresh in your memory.
scenarios.prompt: What does the training identify here, and what is the correct response?
choices: This matches hostile work environment harassment — unwelcome conduct severe or pervasive enough to alter work conditions. Laughing along does not make it welcome, and the correct response is to report through the company's procedure.
It is only harassment if the coworker objects out loud; silent discomfort does not count.
It is a personal problem between them; staying out of it is the professional move.
It only counts as harassment if it happens in writing.
scenarios.why: Harassment training centers on two tests: was the conduct unwelcome, and was it severe or pervasive enough to change the work environment? 'They laughed along' is a classic trap — people mask discomfort to survive at work. Reporting channels exist precisely so one apprentice does not have to confront a senior journeyman alone.
scenarios.hint: Ask who the training says decides whether conduct was welcome — the person doing it, or the person receiving it?

scenarios.title: The First Paycheck Plan
scenarios.situation: You land an apprenticeship at $19/hour and want to avoid the debt spiral you have seen other trades workers fall into. Your budgeting module covered the 50/30/20 rule, APR on revolving credit, and the rule that credit utilization under 30% protects your score.
scenarios.prompt: What is the soundest plan for the first three paychecks?
choices: Budget roughly 50% to needs, 30% to wants, 20% to savings/debt; keep credit-card balances below 30% of the limit and pay revolving balances in full to avoid high APR interest.
Put everything on a credit card to build credit fast, then pay the minimums.
Skip the budget — apprentices do not earn enough for budgeting to matter.
Take a payday loan for tools now and sort out the budget after the first raise.
scenarios.why: The 50/30/20 split is a planning scaffold, not a law, but the math it protects is real: revolving credit at high APR compounds against you, and utilization above 30% drags your score down — exactly when a young worker needs credit for a vehicle or tools. Minimum payments keep you in debt for years; full payoff keeps the card working for you instead of the reverse.
scenarios.hint: Which of these plans has you paying interest to a lender, and which has the lender's product working for you?

scenarios.title: Aptitude Test: Algebra Under Pressure
scenarios.situation: The etA aptitude test includes algebra word problems, including Ohm's law applications. One question reads: 'A 240-volt circuit draws 15 amps. The electrician needs the power in watts and must solve for the unknown in P = V × I, then check the answer against a second formula.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the power, and what does the verification step demonstrate?
choices: 3,600 watts; the verification (e.g., P = I²R after solving R = V/I = 16 Ω, giving 15² × 16 = 3,600 W) demonstrates the aptitude-test skill of checking work with an independent method.
255 watts; verification is unnecessary if you trusted the first formula.
360 watts; multiplication of voltage and current gives watt-hours directly.
36,000 watts; decimal placement does not matter on a multiple-choice test.
scenarios.why: P = V × I gives 240 × 15 = 3,600 W. The independent check matters more than the number: solving R = V/I = 16 Ω and confirming I²R = 225 × 16 = 3,600 W catches the classic slip of multiplying 240 × 15 as 3,600 while misplacing a decimal elsewhere. Aptitude tests are designed to reward learners who verify, because field electrical math has no answer key.
scenarios.hint: Can you solve for resistance first, then get power without ever touching P = V × I? If yes, you have a real check.

lessons.title: Electrician Apprenticeship: etA Entrance — Core concepts
concepts: Interim credentials (OSHA 10, First Aid/CPR, core craft certifications) document job-ready skills while apprenticeship hours accumulate — they never substitute for licensure.
SQ3R (Survey, Question, Read, Recite, Review) turns dense technical documents into retrievable knowledge; the Recite step is where learning actually happens.
Harassment prevention: quid pro quo and hostile work environment are the two legal categories; unwelcomeness is judged from the receiver's side, and reporting procedures protect everyone on the crew.
Core budgeting: the 50/30/20 scaffold, keeping revolving credit utilization under 30%, and paying balances in full to avoid high-APR compounding.
Codes literacy: the NEC is navigated by article structure and index, not memorized; reading exceptions and definitions around a rule is the professional habit.
Algebra readiness: Ohm's law (V = IR) and the power equation (P = VI) are rearrangeable tools — solving for the unknown and verifying with an independent formula is the aptitude-test differentiator.

example.code:
# Ohm's law drill: solve for the unknown, then verify with a second formula
# Given: V = 240 V, I = 15 A. Find P.
P=$(( 240 * 15 ))
echo "P = V x I = $P W"
# Verification: R = V / I = 16 ohm; P = I^2 * R
R=$(( 240 / 15 ))
echo "R = V / I = $R ohm"
echo "Check: P = I^2 x R = $(( 15 * 15 * R )) W"
example.walkthrough: Aptitude-test algebra is about isolating unknowns and cross-checking. Here the primary formula P = V × I gives 3,600 W; solving R = V/I = 16 Ω and confirming P = I²R = 3,600 W proves the arithmetic with an independent path. On a timed test, the 30 seconds spent verifying is cheaper than a careless miss.

pitfalls: Common trap: treating interim credentials as a shortcut to licensure — they document progress; only logged hours plus the license exam qualify you.
Common trap: passive highlighting instead of SQ3R's Recite step — feeling prepared is not the same as retrieving from memory.
Common trap: assuming 'they laughed along' means conduct was welcome — harassment is judged from the receiver's experience and whether it was severe or pervasive.
Common trap: paying only the credit-card minimum — at high APR, minimums service interest first and can keep a balance alive for years.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

labs.title: Ohm's Law Aptitude Drill
labs.objective: Solve ten rapid-fire circuit-math problems using Ohm's law and the power equation, verifying each answer with an independent formula.
steps: Open the drill terminal and note the given values (two of V, I, R, P) for problem 1.
Solve for the unknown using V = IR or P = VI, rearranged as needed.
Verify your answer with the second formula (e.g., if you used P = VI, check with P = I²R).
If the two answers disagree, find the arithmetic error before moving on.
Record your final answer and time for each of the ten problems.
Review your error pattern at the end: decimal slips, wrong rearrangement, or unit mix-ups.

checks.hint: Type solve with your answer; the drill confirms only when both formulas agree.
Type report to summarize your ten problems and error pattern.

labs.title: Code Navigation & Workplace Readiness
labs.objective: Navigate a simulated NEC excerpt to locate rules by article, then walk a harassment-reporting and budgeting checklist.
steps: Use the code index to find the article governing working-space clearances (Article 110) and read its exceptions.
Locate the article on ground-fault protection for personnel (Article 210, GFCI rules) and note the required locations.
Run the SQ3R summary command on a two-page wiring-method excerpt and recite the three main points from memory.
Walk the harassment-reporting chain: identify the reporting contact, the documentation needed, and the anti-retaliation protection.
Build a first-month budget with the 50/30/20 scaffold at apprentice wages and flag the credit-utilization ceiling.
Confirm each step with the check commands below.

checks.hint: Type codefind with the topic; it returns the article and its exceptions.
Type budget with your wage; it builds the 50/30/20 split and the credit ceiling.

sections.title: Electrician Apprenticeship: etA Entrance — entrance path

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you had to learn a dense technical document under time pressure.
behavioral.framework: STAR: Situation (the document and deadline), Task (what you had to extract), Action (your method — e.g., SQ3R), Result (what you retained and how it showed).
points: Name the reading method you used
Show how you verified understanding, not just skimming
Tie the result to a measurable outcome
pitfalls: Saying you just read it twice
No evidence you checked your own understanding

behavioral.prompt: Why do you want to become an electrician, and why the apprenticeship route?
behavioral.framework: Connect personal motivation to the trade's reality: safety, craft, and the earn-while-you-learn structure.
points: Genuine interest in electrical work or building trades
Respect for the multi-year learning path
Long-term goal: journeyman licensure and craft mastery
pitfalls: Saying it is just a paycheck
Suggesting the apprenticeship is a shortcut to licensing

behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you spotted a safety problem and what you did.
behavioral.framework: STAR: what you saw, why it was unsafe, who you told or what you stopped, and the outcome.
points: Specific hazard, not a vague story
Immediate action — stop work, tell a supervisor
Follow-through: confirmed the hazard was fixed
pitfalls: Heroics that bypassed the supervisor
A story with no action taken

behavioral.prompt: How do you handle working under someone with far more experience who is doing something you think is wrong?
behavioral.framework: Respect + safety hierarchy: ask, verify against code/procedure, escalate if safety is at stake.
points: Ask a clarifying question first — you may be missing context
Cite the rule or procedure, not your opinion
Never let deference override a genuine safety concern
pitfalls: Saying you would just go along to keep the peace
Sounding arrogant about your own limited experience

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you made a math or measurement error and how you caught it.
behavioral.framework: STAR with emphasis on the verification step: what the error was, how the check caught it, what you changed.
points: Honesty about the error
A concrete checking habit (second formula, re-measure, peer check)
A system change so it does not recur
pitfalls: Claiming you never make errors
Blaming the tools or the instructions

behavioral.prompt: How would you respond if a coworker was being harassed on a job site?
behavioral.framework: State the principle (everyone deserves a safe workplace), the procedure (report through proper channels), and the support (stand with the coworker, do not retaliate).
points: Knowledge of reporting procedures
Do not confront the harasser alone if unsafe
Document what you observed
pitfalls: Saying it is none of your business
Promising to handle it physically yourself

behavioral.prompt: Apprenticeship wages start modest. How are you planning your finances for the first year?
behavioral.framework: Show a realistic plan: budget structure, tool costs, emergency cushion, credit discipline.
points: A budgeting method (e.g., 50/30/20)
Separating tool investment from lifestyle spending
Avoiding high-interest debt
pitfalls: No plan at all
Depending on future raises to fix current spending

behavioral.prompt: What does a typical day look like when you are balancing classroom instruction with on-the-job training?
behavioral.framework: Walk through time management: prep, site work, evening study, rest — showing you can sustain both tracks.
points: Realistic study blocks, not wishful thinking
Protecting sleep and physical recovery
Using interim credentials and milestones as motivation
pitfalls: Sounding like you will study 'whenever there is time'
Ignoring the physical toll of the trade

cheatsheet: SQ3R: Survey → Question → Read → Recite → Review. Recite (recall from memory) is the learning step.
Interim credentials: OSHA 10, First Aid/CPR, core craft certs — stackable proof while hours accrue; never a license substitute.
Harassment categories: quid pro quo (this-for-that) and hostile work environment (severe or pervasive unwelcome conduct).
50/30/20: ~50% needs, ~30% wants, ~20% savings/debt. Credit utilization under 30%. Pay revolving balances in full.
NEC navigation: use the index → article → read definitions + exceptions. Article 110: general installation requirements; Article 210: branch circuits (GFCI); Article 250: grounding and bonding.
Ohm's law: V = IR. Power: P = VI = I²R = V²/R. Always verify with a second formula.
Well-being: heat illness signs (cramps, dizziness), hydration, sleep, and PPE are job-performance tools, not optional extras.

glossary.def: The electrical training Alliance-style apprenticeship entrance path this module prepares for: classroom instruction plus supervised on-the-job hours toward licensure.
A short, verifiable certification (e.g., OSHA 10, First Aid/CPR) earned during an apprenticeship while license-required hours accumulate.
A five-step study method: Survey, Question, Read, Recite, Review — designed for dense technical material.
National Electrical Code: the reference standard for safe electrical installations in the United States, organized by articles.
National Electrical Contractors Association: a trade association whose standards and practices inform professional electrical work.
National Electrical Manufacturers Representatives Association: an industry association for electrical manufacturers' representatives.
Harassment where a job benefit is conditioned on tolerating unwelcome conduct.
Unwelcome conduct severe or pervasive enough to alter the conditions of employment.
Annual percentage rate: the yearly cost of borrowing on revolving credit, the number to minimize by paying balances in full.
V = IR: voltage equals current times resistance — the foundation of circuit math, rearrangeable to solve for any unknown.

I can navigate the NEC by index → article → exceptions without memorizing article numbers.
I know the difference between quid pro quo and hostile work environment harassment and how to report.
I can build a 50/30/20 budget and explain why credit utilization stays under 30%.
I can solve V=IR and P=VI for any unknown and verify with a second formula.
I can list the interim credentials I am targeting and what each one proves.
